title: The weaver on the steps
hook: a weaver lies on the dark river steps, waiting for a guru's foot
carry: the guru's gift is the name
tomorrow: Kabir sings to Ram. but which Ram?

segments.voice: Yesterday, at Shirdi, Hindus and Muslims came to one saint, each in their own way: darshan follows holiness, not labels. Today, back to Kabir, and the morning he got his teacher's word.

Before dawn in Benares, the ghats, the stone steps down to the Ganga, are still dark. A well-loved legend says a young weaver lay down on those steps on purpose. His name was Kabir, remembered as raised in a Muslim weaving family. He knew a great teacher of Ram, Ramananda, came down to bathe every morning. The old man's foot struck something in the dark, and he cried out: Ram! The weaver got up and went home, saying he'd been given his guru's word. Here's the puzzle. Does that count?
screen: `DARK STEPS, BEFORE DAWN.` → `A FOOT, AND A CRY: RAM!` → `DOES THAT COUNT?`

segments.voice: It's a legend, and it's told as one; historians debate whether the two ever met. But the tradition kept it, and an old garland of saints' lives, the Bhaktamal of Nabhadas, names Kabir among Ramananda's disciples. Why does the story work? Because of a Hindu practice called diksha, initiation. A seeker goes to a guru, and the guru gives a name of God, a mantra, often whispered, often kept private for life. Many bhakti teachers say the name isn't just a label for God; it carries God. So when the guru's own lips say Ram, even by accident, even in the dark, the gift has been given. Kabir sang that name the rest of his life. And notice who got it. Ramananda's circle, as the Bhaktamal remembers it, held a weaver, a leatherworker and a barber. Now the never-blended part. Hindus who took Kabir in didn't need a new religion to explain him. They had their own frame: a guru, a name, a disciple. Muslims who remember Kabir keep their own account of him. Neither rewrote its teaching. And today? Hindus still take diksha, and many families have someone, a grandmother, an uncle, who repeats a name received long ago, quietly, every day.
screen: `A LEGEND, TOLD AS ONE.` · `DIKSHA: THE GURU GIVES A NAME.` · `A HINDU FRAME FOR KABIR.` · then, large: `THE NAME IS THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: This is japa, repeating a name of God, the way Kabir kept Ram's. Choose one: Ram, or a name that's yours, or, if you don't pray, a word you hold dear. Say it softly, once with each out-breath, for the length of the sit. If your mind wanders, there's nothing to fix. Just begin again with the name.
Never blended as doctrine. Here, Kabir takes Ram's name from a Hindu guru, inside a Hindu frame, while Muslims keep their own memory of him.
Keep this: the guru's gift is the name. A weaver on the dark steps received it. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Hindus receive diksha, initiation, from a guru, who gives a mantra or name of God that the disciple repeats in japa and often keeps private; the legend of Kabir receiving Ram's name from Ramananda is a well-loved telling of it.

fork.reveal: In the legend, a weaver from a Muslim family took Ram's name from a guru's lips. Traditions differ, but in many, diksha is about the name given.
